name: Castor oil
lead: Castor oil is a thick, pale vegetable oil pressed from the seeds of the castor plant, Ricinus communis, and about 90 percent of its fatty acids are ricinoleate [1]. It has been used for more than three millennia as a laxative and today is also an industrial raw material, a cosmetic emollient and a carrier in medicines [1][8].

In looksmaxxing and hair-care communities it is used as a topical oil on the scalp, beard, eyebrows and eyelashes. Proponents apply it nightly with a brush or fingertips, hoping for fuller-looking brows and lashes, thicker-looking hair and a conditioned shine; its viscosity also makes it a styling and sealing oil for some users [4][6][17]. Some combine it with rosemary oil, minoxidil or derma stamping, and some pair it with a prescription lash product [2][5][4].

A 2022 systematic review of coconut, castor and argan oils for hair in skin-of-colour patients covered 22 articles; it reported weaker evidence for castor oil improving hair luster and no strong evidence for growth, and noted that dermatologists often let patients continue hair oils because side effects are unlikely [9]. No clinical trial of castor oil for eyebrow, eyelash or scalp hair growth has been published [1][9].
Its established medical use is oral, as a stimulant laxative; the US label for an over-the-counter product lists temporary relief of occasional constipation [3].

paras: Castor oil is colourless to pale yellow with a distinct taste and odour, and it is unusually viscous for a vegetable oil [1]. Its triglycerides are dominated by ricinoleic acid, a hydroxylated fatty acid, with oleic and linoleic acids as the other notable components [1][8]. The hydroxyl group is what gives the oil its thickness, its stickiness on skin and its usefulness as a chemical feedstock [2][8].

Retail products come in several forms: plain pressed oil, solvent-free cold-pressed oil, and oil from roasted beans, often sold as Jamaican or 'black' castor oil. Hydrogenated castor oil appears as a thickener in personal-care products [1].

Castor oil is recorded as a laxative in the Ebers Papyrus, dated about 1550 BC, and was likely used earlier [1]. Its laxative action is attributed to ricinoleic acid released during digestion [1]. Nineteenth-century midwifery manuals recommended it for 'false pains', and it is still used for labour induction where modern drugs are unavailable [1].

Industrially it is a bio-based polyol for polyurethanes, coatings and foams, a precursor for chemicals such as sebacic acid and nylon-11 monomer, a low-temperature lubricant, a biodiesel feedstock and, historically, the main lubricant of First World War rotary aircraft engines [1][8]. The Turkey red oil derived from it was the first synthetic detergent after soap [1]. Food-grade forms serve as additives and in chocolate manufacture [1]. It is also a vehicle for some injected medicines [1].

A randomized trial examined topical periocular castor oil treatment for blepharitis, an eyelid condition [13]. Registered trials for castor oil concern labour induction and dental pulp response [14][15].

Cosmetically it acts as an emollient and carrier in lipsticks, hair conditioners and creams [1][2]. Wikipedia's overview of hair conditioners notes that natural oils have conditioned hair for centuries, and that modern products have largely replaced simple oils with silicones, fatty alcohols and polymers [7].

Hair oiling is a long-standing practice in Indian and African-heritage communities, and castor, coconut and argan oils are the commercially popular choices [9]. The 2022 review describes these oils as culturally rooted, and notes that dermatologists frequently advise continued use because adverse effects are rarely foreseen [9].

In looksmaxxing forums the oil is applied to eyebrows and eyelashes with a clean spoolie or mascara wand, to the beard and scalp as a massage oil, and sometimes to hair ends for gloss. Users often describe the routine as a low-cost companion to other hair or brow measures [4][5][11][12].

Proponents offer several explanations: that the oil moisturises and seals the shaft so hair breaks less, that massage improves scalp circulation, that ricinoleic acid has anti-inflammatory action and that the thick coating makes strands read as darker and denser. A looksmax.org thread title goes further and calls castor oil a 'legit collagen booster' [16]. These are users' proposals; the 2022 dermatology review found no strong evidence of growth effects [9].
For labour induction, a 2024 review said the mechanism is poorly understood and that a prostaglandin pathway has been suggested but not confirmed [1][10].

Taken by mouth, castor oil commonly causes nausea, vomiting, cramping and diarrhoea, and medical guidance discourages its use for simple constipation [1]. The US label advises against use when abdominal pain, nausea or vomiting are present unless directed by a doctor [3]. A pregnancy drug reference advises against oral or topical use in women who are pre-term pregnant [1].

Castor beans contain ricin, a toxic lectin, but heating during extraction deactivates it and it is not present in the finished oil [1][2]. A toxicology review describes ricin as dangerous mainly by inhalation or injection, with poor oral absorption and absorption through intact skin considered very unlikely [11]. The bean also contains an allergen, CB1A, that is neutralised during processing and is not in the oil [1].

Topical hair-use safety has not been the subject of dedicated trials; the review of hair oils states that side effects are not foreseen for these oils [9]. The American Cancer Society says evidence does not support claims that topical castor oil cures cancer or other diseases [1].

Seeds contain roughly 30 to 60 percent oil depending on source, and the oil is obtained by pressing or solvent extraction [1][2]. India is the largest producer [2]. A 1995 PNAS paper identified the oleate 12-hydroxylase enzyme in castor endosperm that creates ricinoleic acid, and a 2010 Nature Biotechnology paper published the plant's draft genome [12][18].

On looksmax.org, castor oil is most often discussed for eyebrows and eyelashes, sometimes combined with rosemary oil, minoxidil or derma stamping. Reports are mixed: one user described a month of nightly use followed by visibly longer lashes and a friend noticing thicker brows [6], while others report barely noticeable changes after a year [4]. A third thread acknowledges no strong evidence while suggesting it may at least coat brows like mascara [5]. Users also describe its thickness as awkward to apply [6].

Thread titles over several years show that the topic recurs: castor oil for eyelashes, castor oil with minoxidil, castor oil and derma stamping, castor oil for styling, and a post arguing it is 'the most misunderstood looksmax' that disparages minoxidil [19][20][21][22][23]. Both 'castor oil is legit' and 'castor oil is cope' positions are posted as thread titles [24][6][5].

No studies found on castor oil for hair, eyebrow or eyelash growth. A 2022 systematic review of 22 articles on coconut, castor and argan hair oils reported weaker evidence for castor oil improving hair luster, no strong evidence for hair growth, and no strong evidence for treating infestation; for coconut oil it found clinical evidence for brittle hair and infestation [9].

Registered clinical trials listed for castor oil concern labour induction in post-date pregnancy, including after previous caesarean, and dental pulp response [14][15]. A systematic review of three trials in 233 women reported insufficient evidence on labour induction, with all women taking it orally feeling nauseous [1]. A 2024 review of induction methods lists castor oil among complementary approaches [10]. A randomized trial studied it topically on the eyelid margins for blepharitis [13].

lore.intro: Castor oil appears repeatedly in hair, brow and lash threads on looksmax.org as a cheap topical growth aid, often debated as 'legit' or 'cope'. [4][5][6][24]

claims.claim: Castor oil thickens brows and lengthens lashes.
claims.believers: Some users report noticeable lash growth after about a month of nightly application, and a friend noticing thicker brows. [6]
claims.experts: No published trial has tested castor oil for brow or lash growth. [1][9]

claims.claim: Castor oil barely works compared with other options.
claims.believers: Other users say a year of use, even with minoxidil on brows, produced barely noticeable change, and that a prescription lash product did more. [4]
claims.experts: No trials compare castor oil against these treatments. [1]

claims.claim: It is harmless even if the effect is unproven, since it coats hair like mascara.
claims.believers: One user says there is no strong evidence it works but it does no harm and acts like mascara. [5]
claims.experts: Dermatologists in a 2022 review note that hair oils are often continued because side effects are not foreseen; the label warnings concern oral use. [9][3]

claims.claim: Castor oil improves hair shine and quality.
claims.believers: Users describe softer, glossier hair and brows after oiling. [6]
claims.experts: The 2022 systematic review described weaker evidence that castor oil improves hair luster. [9]

claims.claim: Castor oil is a 'legit collagen booster' and a better option than minoxidil.
claims.believers: Thread titles on looksmax.org make these claims, one arguing castor oil is the most misunderstood looksmax and that minoxidil is inferior. [16][19]
claims.experts: No published human trial has examined castor oil for collagen or compared it with minoxidil; minoxidil is the subject of separate randomized trials. [9]

claims.claim: The ricin in castor beans makes the oil dangerous to use on skin.
claims.believers: Some people worry about the toxin because of the plant's reputation.
claims.experts: The oil is made from heat-treated seed, and a toxicology review says ricin is poorly absorbed orally and absorption through intact skin is very unlikely. [1][11]

claims.claim: Castor oil taken orally is a safe way to cleanse the gut or induce labour.
claims.believers: Folk and midwifery traditions have used it for both for generations. [1]
claims.experts: Reviews report insufficient evidence for labour induction, frequent nausea, and advise against its use for simple constipation. [1][10]

card.summary: A thick pressed seed oil people rub on hair, brows and lashes; established as a laxative, untested for growth.
card.note: Oral use causes cramping and diarrhoea; no hair-growth trials found.

quick.overview:
Castor oil is a viscous oil pressed from castor beans. It is sold as an over-the-counter laxative and used in cosmetics and industry.
Looksmaxxers apply it to scalp, brows and lashes hoping for thicker growth. Users report mixed results, and no clinical trials on hair growth were found.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say it moisturises and thickens strands. Its main component, ricinoleic acid, makes it very viscous. A hair-growth mechanism has not been shown.
quick.risks: Taken orally it commonly causes nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea, and labels advise against use with abdominal pain. A pregnancy reference advises against use in pre-term pregnancy. Ricin from the raw bean is not in the processed oil.

chain: Oil is brushed onto scalp, brows or lashes
It coats the strands, adding shine, slip and a thicker appearance
Brows and lashes look darker and fuller; users also hope for growth
angle.text: People brush castor oil onto brows, lashes, beard or scalp as a cheap nightly routine. Its immediate effect is conditioning and gloss, which can make hair look fuller; whether it changes growth is the claim users debate.
